patterns: highly predictable next word in a fixed formulaic phrase or collocation (e.g. 'motion [for]', 'data are represented [as]', 'thank you very [much]', 'recommended [that]', 'I [respectfully] dissent', 'something [like] this')

Tokens strongly predictable from context or memorized sequences. This covers idiom completions ("all of its own", "worth their salt", "to say the least", "top of his game", "tears in our eyes") and continuations of known Latin, drug or chemical names (oxysporum, carotovora, methotrexate, edulis). It also covers fixed boilerplate or format continuations such as pangrams, patent phrasing ("may"), script speaker colons and LaTeX.

positions inside coordinated lists or enumerations where another item is expected next: a comma or token before the next list item, the closing ref-type="table"/"fig" before "and [N", and "respectively" after paired items; a few snippets are noise

predictable next word that completes a fixed formulaic phrase (e.g. 'motion [for]', 'Data are represented [as]', 'Thank you very [much]', 'recommended [that]', 'something [like]', 'I [respectfully] dissent')
common in legal, scientific-methods and polite conversational boilerplate
media/communication channel words (Twitter, online, radio, email, social media, Facebook, YouTube, Internet, WhatsApp)
offshoots: punctuation and tokens within fixed multi-word compounds/identifiers (commas in lists, mid-word fragments in code/names)
token that closes off a noun phrase or constituent before the sentence continues: the final piece of a multi-token name or word (Legislation, Brake, HindIII, 3rd)
a comma or closing parenthesis ending a modifier or relative clause
a coordinating 'and' or 'or' joining noun phrases
a preposition or relativizer attaching to a just-completed noun phrase
tokens that open a phrase needing a following complement, strongest in acknowledgments: 'thank', 'grateful/indebted to'
fixed openers like 'Due (to)', 'In spite (of)', 'Because', 'Pursuant'
similar complement slots in other languages and code: French elided l', '#include', PHP 'use', 'whose', possessive 's'

Main job: the word that comes right after a clause's subject, usually an auxiliary, modal or verb. Typical cases are "you['ll]" and "you [will]" after an if-clause or a generic statement, "there['s]", "there [are]" and "there [exists]", and "X [must]" ("Redistributions in binary form must", "a complaint must").
Related offshoot in code: the keyword that comes next in a fixed SQL pattern, as in "SELECT * [FROM]", plus WHERE, AND, and "match x [with]".
Offshoot: the % sign after 95 in statistics ("95[%] CI", "95[%] cover").

Weaker scattered hits on other fairly predictable continuations such as "all", "within", "outweigh" and "....". It is not a general predictable-token detector: "United States" and the "would" in "they would" barely fire.

token right before an alphanumeric identifier or designation number, especially the period in 'No.' in legal citations (Docket No., S.Rep.No., Exh. No.), plus labels like Form, Interstate, Rule, Patent No., Protocol Number, and the c. in mutation codes
weaker offshoot: a repeated identifier or symbol in parallel code or math structure (a.Count || b.Count, \alpha_1 + \alpha_2, \overline{...})

predictable completion of a stock phrase in formal, procedural or polite language: the word that finishes a verb's or noun's set wording (represented AS, motion FOR, recommend THAT, with respect TO, thank you very MUCH, I RESPECTFULLY dissent, performed at VARIOUS)

tokens that complete highly predictable stock phrases or fixed templates (legal citation terms like 'cert. denied' and 'S.Ct.', travel-guide prices and opening hours, phone numbers like 0800, collocations like 'a year ago' and 'spilled everything')

head of the predicate right after a subject: verbs/auxiliaries after a noun-phrase subject (buses ... stop, the callback returns, beer can) and especially adjectives in 'it is ___ to/for/that' frames (it is common/rare/fair/easy to)
